title: Refresh by relocation shuffles row-hammer adjacencies every window
idea: Reverse refresh from restore-in-place into move: each refresh slot copies one row into a spare row in the same subarray (in-array row copy through the shared sense amps) and updates a small remap table, so within each window every row is both refreshed and physically relocated. An attacker can no longer keep hammering the same physical neighbors, so extra target-row refreshes become unnecessary.
why: Merges regular and mitigation refresh (facts 3, 9), recovering ~10-30% of refresh-related bandwidth at ~1k hammer thresholds for ~1 spare row per subarray.

title: Trim the tail: charge-trap access transistors programmed at test
idea: Reverse a flash technique into a DRAM fix: build access transistors with an ONO (SONOS) charge-trap gate stack in an existing 40-65 nm embedded-SONOS fab. At wafer test, measure each cell's retention and give the tail cells (~0.01-1%) a one-time program pulse that raises their Vt ~200 mV and cuts their leakage 10-100x, folding the tail into the bulk distribution.
why: Refresh is set by the tail (fact 3); trimming it allows 64 ms to ~256 ms+ refresh (4x+) on existing trailing-node eSONOS lines; wordline disturb of the trap layer is the risk.

title: Keithley driven-guard cell: a follower nulls access-transistor Vds
idea: Revive the electrometer's driven guard, which kills leakage by holding a node's surroundings at the node's own voltage: split the access path into two series transistors with a tiny cell-local node between them. A zero-Vt native source follower from the storage node drives that local node, so the inner transistor sees Vds near 0 in hold and its subthreshold leakage falls by orders of magnitude.
why: Directly attacks the subthreshold part of the tail (fact 3): 10-100x longer retention for 1.5-2x cell area, which is worth it in a refresh-free tier.

title: 1968 zinc-oxide TFT revived as indium- and gallium-free access device
idea: Revive Boesen and Jacobs' 1968 ZnO thin-film transistor with modern ALD: an amorphized nitrogen/Mg-alloyed ZnO channel, using zinc from Alaska and Tennessee, forms BEOL access transistors with ultralow off-current from its 3.3 eV gap. It avoids IGZO's indium and gallium, both refined mostly abroad.
why: Oxide-semiconductor-level leakage gives multi-second retention (fact 3), with an all-U.S. element supply and BEOL stacking (fact 2).

title: Gecko-feet dry transfer of 2D access channel sheets
idea: Random stimulus 'gecko feet': stick and release by van der Waals forces, no glue. Grow wafer-scale WSe2/MoS2 on a sapphire donor, pick it up with a dry thermal-release stamp and laminate it onto the BEOL storage-capacitor array, forming the access transistors with ALD gates above the capacitors so the array needs no FEOL silicon access module.
why: Atomically thin, ~2 eV-gap channels give sub-fA off current (fact 3); replacing ~20 FEOL wet loops with one dry transfer plus ALD cuts access-module water >10x, and the sapphire donor is reusable.

title: Electric-fence gate isolation replaces oxide-filled array STI
idea: Random stimulus 'electric fence': a field keeps the herd apart with no wall. Isolate adjacent access transistors with dedicated always-off isolation-gate lines held at -0.5 V in shallow recesses, in place of deep oxide-filled STI that needs fill, CMP and repeated HF recess dips.
why: Removes the array STI fill-CMP-recess wet loop (>10x less water in that module) and frees area for a wider channel; the isolation gate is placed and biased to shield neighbors rather than hammer them (facts 3, 9).

title: Gallium-oxide thin-film access transistors with 4.8 eV bandgap
idea: Po: the access transistor is made from an insulator. Deposit Ga2O3 by low-temperature ALD with laser crystallization as the access channel; its 4.8 eV gap makes thermal generation negligible, targeting off-current near 1e-21 A per cell, well below IGZO.
why: Fact 3: ~100x lower tail than IGZO and ~1e7x below Si, allowing hour-scale refresh and smaller capacitors (fact 1); risk is ~10 cm2/Vs mobility and contact resistance.

title: Gardener's graft: transistor-last access devices on transferred crystal silicon
idea: A gardener grafts a healthy scion onto rootstock. Build the capacitor array first at its full thermal budget, then bond and smart-cut a pristine 50 nm single-crystal Si layer on top and form access transistors at <=500 C with in-situ-doped, laser-activated junctions, so no capacitor anneal ever crosses the junctions and no implant damage seeds traps.
why: Implant damage and thermal cycling seed the leakage tail; a damage-free low-thermal-budget junction could improve tail retention 3-10x, and decoupling capacitor and transistor processes also eases the 3D DRAM blocker (fact 2).

title: Cerium-oxide redox buffer pins oxide-channel stoichiometry for years-stable Vt
idea: Ce: cap DUV-patterned zinc-tin-oxide access transistors with a few-nm CeOx layer whose reversible Ce3+/Ce4+ couple absorbs or releases oxygen and hydrogen, buffering the channel's oxygen chemical potential so bias-stress and hydrogen-driven Vt drift, which raises off-current over life, is suppressed with no added lithography.
why: Oxide access devices deliver ultra-low leakage only if Vt stays put; stable Vt preserves seconds-scale retention (fact 3) over product life and makes relaxed-pitch BEOL DRAM viable without EUV.

title: Lab-grown-gem CVD diamond access transistors with 5.5 eV channels
idea: Reuse the U.S. lab-grown diamond industry's CVD reactors to grow thin single-crystal diamond tiers. Build H-terminated surface-channel access FETs on them, using transfer-doping oxide such as MoO3 to switch the channel on.
why: Zero refresh: intrinsic generation in 5.5 eV diamond is effectively nil and junctionless surface channels remove GIDL, giving retention of years. This also creates a domestic, non-EUV memory supply chain.

title: Anodized aluminum capacitor forest: 1000:1 aspect ratio for free
idea: Inverts 'high-aspect-ratio capacitors need costly etch': anodize thick aluminum to self-organize vertical pores at ~40-60 nm pitch and ~1000:1 aspect ratio, then ALD-line them with TiN/ZrO2/TiN, giving tens of fF per cell so that cheap, leaky TFT access devices still retain for seconds.
why: Breaks the capacitor charge wall (fact 1) without deep RIE or EUV and lets low-cost leaky access meet retention (fact 3); stacked with TFT tiers, claimed ~100x cost/GB; trade-off is larger pitch and slower bitline sensing.

title: Quadrant-gated pillars: four lateral storage pockets per tier
idea: IFR: one bitline pillar serves every direction. Around each vertical bitline pillar, split the tier wordline into four independently driven quadrant gates, each gating a short lateral oxide channel to its own storage pocket, so each pillar holds four cells per tier.
why: Constraint: 4 cells per pillar per tier across ~16 tiers is ~64 bits per pillar footprint, >10x density per wafer, while bitline contacts drop 4x.

title: Post-fab Vt healing of tail access transistors via trap-layer programming
idea: Random dopant and trap fluctuations put a few transistors per billion 4-5 sigma low in Vt, and their subthreshold current dominates the tail. Add a thin SiN charge-trap layer in the buried-wordline liner. At wafer test, find the short-retention cells and inject electrons into only their gate stacks (high wordline voltage, their bitline driven, neighbors inhibited) to raise their Vt ~200 mV.
why: At ~70 mV/dec, +200 mV cuts a tail cell's subthreshold leakage ~700x. That collapses the distribution toward the median and allows a 4-8x longer refresh interval (fact 3).

title: Lifetime-matched no-refresh regions hold short-lived AI tensors
idea: Effect: exponential RC charge decay used as a free timer. A new mode register and allocator hint expose per-bank refresh-off regions; the runtime places activations, KV-cache scratch and gradient buffers that live <32 ms there (each write restores charge), so those rows are never refreshed.
why: Refresh bandwidth and energy (fact 3): with 50-80% of accelerator DRAM traffic short-lived, removes refresh for those regions (10-20% bandwidth at 32-64 Gb); needs controller/OS changes.

title: Nicotinic coincidence-gated access FET opens only with row AND column
idea: The nicotinic receptor opens only when two acetylcholine molecules bind; give each BEOL access FET two independent gates (top on the wordline, bottom on a column-segment select line) with Vt set so neither alone inverts the channel.
why: Only the 64-256 requested bits are activated instead of an 8 KB page, ending the 128x overfetch and destructive restore (~5.9 to <1 pJ/useful bit); victims see only partial activations (less row hammer); refresh can be segmented by column.

title: Electric double layer storage: ions replace the solid dielectric
idea: Inverts 'the storage dielectric must be a solid insulator': use a nanometre-thin solid polymer or ionogel electrolyte between ion-blocking electrodes so the electric double layer gives ~10-30 uF/cm2 (3-6x high-k ZrO2); blocking electrodes keep DC leakage low and nanoscale thickness keeps the ionic RC short.
why: Breaks the capacitor charge wall (fact 1: AR 60-75:1 -> ~15:1) and buys retention margin against access leakage (fact 3); risk is ionic switching speed at ns scale.

title: LiPON ionic back-gate puts idle subarrays into deep-Vt hibernation
idea: Li: put a thin-film-battery-style LiPON electrolyte plus Li reservoir under each subarray, separated from the silicon by an Al2O3 Li-blocking liner; a ~1 V, ~10 ms pulse builds an ionic double layer that shifts access-transistor Vt up ~0.3-0.5 V for subarrays idle for seconds, and is reversed before reactivation.
why: Idle refresh is 16-33% of idle power (fact 3); a 0.4 V Vt lift cuts subthreshold leakage ~10^4-10^5, so cold pages need ~100x fewer refreshes on OS-idle timescales.

title: Ban all implants: fixed-charge dielectrics electrostatically dope the access transistor
idea: Limit: no dopant atom may be implanted near the storage node. Fixed charge in the spacer dielectric induces the source/drain extensions instead: positive-charge SiNx for n-type, negative-charge Al2O3 for p-type. The result is an atomically abrupt, damage-free 'junction' with no random dopant fluctuation and no end-of-range defects to act as SRH generation centers.
why: Fact 3: implant damage and dopant clusters seed the high-leakage tail. Removing them could pull worst-cell leakage from ~13 fA toward the median, ~10x, and the refresh interval would stretch accordingly.

title: Move the data, not the amplifier: circulating CCD ring memory
idea: Reverse the access pattern: store bits as charge packets in short rings (32-64 positions) of buried-channel charge-transfer gates, so each packet passes a regenerating sense amplifier once per lap (~20-30 ns at 2 GHz during traffic, slowed to a crawl when idle). Refresh happens on every lap, random access waits at most one lap, and the buried channel under each gate is the storage well, so no capacitor pillar is needed.
why: Makes refresh intrinsic (fact 3) and removes the capacitor (facts 1, 2); latency stays in the 10-30 ns DRAM class; clocking energy and ~2-3 gates per bit are the risks.

title: Leakage-controlled oscillator sets Arrhenius-tracking refresh rate
idea: Worse at 125 C: refresh at a fixed rate chosen for the hottest day of a 10-year life. Flip: drive the refresh timer from an oscillator whose capacitor is charged by the off-current of a replica access transistor, so the refresh rate follows real leakage from -40 to 125 C and with aging.
why: Refresh energy (fact 3) down 4-8x across most of the temperature range while staying safe at 125 C.

title: Window-frame thermal break: keep HBM 25C cooler than its GPU
idea: Aluminum window frames got a polymer thermal break so cold never bridges to the warm side. Cut a low-conductivity trench (porous oxide or sealed void) through the interposer between the GPU and HBM footprints and give HBM its own colder coolant branch, holding DRAM near 60 C instead of 85-95 C.
why: Leakage roughly doubles per ~10 C and refresh doubles above 85 C; 25 C cooler cuts refresh ~4-6x and frees bandwidth (facts 3, 5).

title: Route chilled-water inlet to DRAM first for retention-tiered cooling
idea: Po: DRAM lives in a refrigerator. Re-plumb liquid-cooled AI racks so the coldest inlet water (~15 C) crosses DRAM cold plates before the GPUs, holding arrays near 25 C instead of 85 C, and have the controller apply temperature-compensated refresh tables that stretch tREFI as leakage halves every ~10 C.
why: Fact 3: junction leakage falls ~30-60x from 85 C to 25 C, so refresh interval can stretch 8-16x, recovering most of the 10-20% bandwidth tax and idle refresh power at near-zero capex.

title: Embargoed Soviet tube engineer: vacuum-nanogap field-emission access switch
idea: Soviet designers kept vacuum tubes in the MiG-25 because they shrugged off radiation. Put the storage node behind a sealed 10-20 nm vacuum cavity facing a sharp metal emitter tip; the wordline gate raises the tip field to switch on field-emission current, and with the gate low the gap has no carriers, no junction and no trap states to leak through.
why: Off-state leakage, set by Fowler-Nordheim emission at low field, is effectively zero (<1e-21 A), removing refresh; it is also radiation-hard and needs no high-purity crystalline channel.

title: Tunneling-mode NEMS access switch: vacuum gap replaces the leaky channel
idea: Start from the lowest-leakage switch physics allows: a vacuum gap, where off-current falls about 10x per angstrom of tunneling distance. Replace the access MOSFET with an electrostatically pulled 3 nm SiC nanobeam in a hermetically sealed cavity that moves from a 4 nm gap to a ~0.5 nm non-contact tunneling gap. It never touches, so there is no stiction or wear. Near-gap tunneling easily supplies the ~0.5 uA a 5 fF write in 10 ns needs, while the open-gap current is below 1e-21 A.
why: Removes subthreshold, GIDL and junction leakage in one move, so the 13 fA tail (fact 3) disappears. Retention becomes limited by the capacitor dielectric (minutes to hours), cutting refresh energy and the 10-20% bandwidth tax by >100x.

title: Bubble memory's rotating field drives skyrmion loops, no transistors
idea: Magnetic bubble memory died because long serial loops made access slow. Keep its best trick, one global rotating field that moves every bit so no bit needs its own transistor, and fix the latency. Use 64-bit skyrmion loops in thin multilayer rings, each with one sense MTJ, clocked by an on-chip stripline field so that any bit arrives within 64 steps.
why: The array has no access-transistor leakage and needs no refresh because it is nonvolatile, and density comes from cell-free tracks. Step speed and drive energy are the speculative parts.

title: Micrometer-screw tunneling-gap shutter switches without any contact
idea: A nanocantilever, positioned like a precision micrometer screw, moves the bitline electrode from a 0.5 nm tunnel gap (on) to a 3 nm gap (off) above a metal storage node. It never touches, so there is no stiction or contact wear.
why: Zero refresh: tunneling current falls ~exp(-2kd), about 10^10x from on to off, so off-leakage drops below 1e-24 A and retention lasts years. The non-contact design improves endurance over relays.

title: Use the spare rows already inside: host-driven PPR for weak rows
idea: 10-person constraint: only JEDEC commands. DDR5 exposes host-initiated soft and hard post-package repair. Firmware runs the retention profile, then uses hPPR to fuse the worst row in each bank onto the die's own spare rows (and sPPR for temporary fixes), so the weakest rows physically leave the array before refresh is relaxed.
why: Fact 3: one worst row often sets each bank's refresh interval. Removing it raises the bank minimum by ~1.5-2x with firmware alone.

title: Wine taster's sip: non-destructive subthreshold current read without restore
idea: A taster sips; she never drains the bottle. The wordline rises only to a subthreshold 'sip' level for ~2 ns; the storage-node voltage modulates the access device's subthreshold current exponentially, and a current-mode sense amp on a bitline held at mid reads it while drawing <1% of stored charge; a per-row read counter triggers a full restore only after ~50 sips.
why: Removes the full bitline swing and destructive-read restore (fact 8) from most reads with a ~1 V sip wordline, cutting read access energy ~10x.

title: Tail removal allowed only after packaging: wordline Joule self-anneal
idea: Limit: the leakage tail must be fixed in the field, not in the fab. In maintenance windows, drive a controlled current through segmented wordline straps to Joule-heat a few-um2 region to ~300 C for microseconds. This anneals variable-retention-time trap configurations and redistributes hydrogen at the access transistor's Si/SiO2 interface; the weak rows are then re-profiled.
why: Fact 3: VRT traps drive the 13 fA tail and its unpredictability. Periodic in-situ annealing could shrink the tail ~3-10x over life and allow longer refresh. Risk: thermal stress on neighboring cells.

title: Thermostat-dial controller trades refresh rate for cooling water hourly
idea: Random stimulus 'thermostat dial': one knob, two costs. The memory controller publishes a live curve of refresh overhead versus HBM temperature; the facility's cooling optimizer runs memory hotter (refresh doubles per ~10 C) during hot afternoons instead of switching cooling towers to evaporative mode, and lets memory cool down on cool nights.
why: Spending a few watts of extra refresh (fact 3) to stay in dry-cooling mode through peak hours avoids most evaporative hours; memory cooling water falls >10x in temperate climates using existing chips.

title: Canary rows with undersized capacitors gate refresh timing
idea: A mask change gives a few rows per subarray ~70% of normal capacitance, and they are written with a known pattern. A background sampler issues refresh only when canaries start to flip, so the rate tracks real temperature, voltage and aging.
why: 64 ms is a worst-case guardband while typical retention is seconds, so 4-10x fewer refreshes are possible safely.

title: Wine merchant's vintages: retention-binned DRAM dies sold by grade
idea: Wine is sold by vintage, not poured away for missing Grand Cru. Test every die at 32/64/128/256 ms retention and sell grades: long-retention dies at a premium for phones and laptops, and dies that fail 64 ms (scrapped or heavily repaired today) as 'short-retention' parts run at 16 ms refresh in cache-like or CXL-pool roles.
why: Raises usable supply by recovering dies lost to the retention tail (several % yield) and earns a premium on long-retention dies for low-power markets.

title: Voltage-sensor-helix cooperative gate for steep-slope access transistors
idea: Sodium channels switch at ~5 mV/decade because ~12 gating charges on the S4 helices move together; mimic this by inserting a thin antiferroelectric ZrO2-rich layer into the access-transistor gate stack, tuned so its field-induced phase transition coincides with threshold and gives internal voltage gain (~30 mV/dec over 3-4 decades).
why: At fixed on-current Vt can rise ~150-200 mV, cutting off-current tail 100-1000x (refresh interval >10x), or VPP can drop from ~3 V to ~2 V for ~55% less wordline CV2 energy.

title: Second-reference sense amp flags decaying cells during refresh
idea: Each refresh fires an extra comparator with a tighter reference (~60% of a full 1). Rows with cells below it go to a small fast-refresh list, and the base rate slows until flags appear.
why: Online, self-calibrating multi-rate refresh that catches VRT cells, with 60-80% fewer refreshes, using circuits from the 1990s.

title: Dopant-free Schottky source/drain unlocks 64-tier lateral 3D DRAM
idea: IFR: the lateral transistor in each tier needs no implant. Through the vertical slit, recess each deposited Si or oxide tier and convert the exposed ends into dopant-segregated metal/silicide Schottky contacts, so all 64 tiers get source and drain in one conformal step instead of impossible deep implants.
why: Constraint: removes fact 2's lateral-transistor blocker; 64 tiers from one slit etch give >10x bits per wafer at ~2x cost, and a high storage-side Schottky barrier also lowers off-leakage.

title: Tail bounty: pay for decades of worst-cell leakage cut
idea: Reverse the research metric from median to tail: a CHIPS-funded open prize pays per decade of 1-ppm-tail off-current reduction, measured on standard 1 Mb access-transistor test arrays built on shared 130/65 nm multi-project-wafer shuttles at existing U.S. foundries. Winning device recipes are licensed to DRAM makers.
why: Targets the ~13 fA tail that sets refresh (fact 3) with many cheap university and startup experiments on existing trailing-node shuttles instead of new fabs.

title: Unihemispheric-sleep twin subarrays hide refresh behind mirror reads
idea: Dolphins sleep one brain hemisphere at a time; mirror the hottest ~3-5% of rows into twin subarrays of the same bank so reads hit the awake copy while the other copy refreshes, with writes posted to both or tracked by a dirty bit.
why: Removes refresh-induced stalls for hot data (inference tail latency) for +10-15% effective bandwidth at 64 Gb, at a 3-5% capacity cost.

title: Diffusive silver-filament selector blocks access transistor subthreshold leakage
idea: Effect: electrochemical ion migration with spontaneous filament dissolution. A 3 nm SiOxNy:Ag layer in the storage-node contact forms a filament within ns when the open access transistor applies 0.5-1 V across it, then self-dissolves within ~1 us after the wordline closes, leaving an insulating gap (<1 aA) in series with the transistor's leakage tail.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): series ion gap claims 100x retention. Risk: 1e15 endurance and post-write dissolution window.

title: Eliminate permanent tail cells: in-field Joule self-heating anneal of traps
idea: Drive a short high-current pulse through each gate-all-around nanowire access device, or use its wordline as a resistive heater, to reach ~500-700 C locally for microseconds and re-passivate the defects that cause variable retention time. Repeat periodically in the field to heal aging-induced leakage.
why: Heals the tail cells that dictate refresh, shrinking tail leakage ~10x (fact 3); demonstrable on university-fab nanowires with a probe station.

title: Grounded shield rail kills passing-wordline leakage into storage nodes
idea: In buried-wordline arrays each storage node sits beside a neighboring row's 'passing' wordline. When that line pulses to ~3 V, its fringing field induces leakage and electron injection into the node, the same coupling behind row hammer. Insert a thin grounded conductive rail (doped poly or TiN) in the isolation trench between the passing wordline and the storage node to terminate the field lines.
why: This removes the access-dependent leakage that shortens effective retention under heavy traffic and raises the ~1k row-hammer threshold. Refresh then needs no guardband for neighbor activity (facts 3, 9).

title: SiGe quantum-well hole pocket replaces capacitor in each tier
idea: IFR: the transistor body is itself a leak-proof bucket. In epitaxial Si/SiGe/Si superlattice tiers, holes are stored in a buried compressively strained Ge-rich quantum well under each lateral channel; the ~0.3-0.5 eV valence-band offset confines them and their charge shifts channel Vt for non-destructive reads.
why: Constraint: capacitorless 1T cells at ~30 nm tier pitch allow ~100 epi tiers with NAND-like per-tier cost, aiming >10x density per wafer.

title: Deuterium passivation of junction traps to shrink leakage tail
idea: IFR: no trap ever helps an electron hop. Replace the final forming-gas anneal with a high-pressure deuterium anneal so access-device interface and junction dangling bonds are capped by Si-D bonds, which resist thermal and hot-carrier dissociation far better than Si-H (kinetic isotope effect).
why: Fact 3: trap-assisted tunneling forms the retention tail and variable retention time; a cleaner, more stable tail could double the refresh interval for one anneal change.

title: $1 IoT sensor log repaired by signal smoothness, not ECC
idea: Cheap sensor nodes log slow physical signals (temperature, vibration, ECG). Their embedded 1T1C macro has no ECC and refreshes only at its 1%-BER age (seconds); firmware delta-encodes samples and a Hampel/median filter at read removes physically impossible isolated jumps, using the signal's physics as the code.
why: Cost and fact 3: an ECC-free, rarely refreshed embedded DRAM replaces SRAM at ~5x density in low-cost MCUs, and refresh, often the sleep-power floor, nearly vanishes.

title: Ice-cube-tray GaP storage junction lattice-matched to silicon
idea: Random stimulus 'ice cube tray': each cube sits inside a wall of a different material. Grow the storage-node-side source/drain of the access transistor as epitaxial GaP (2.26 eV gap, within 0.4% of silicon's lattice constant), so the junction where charge leaks has ~1e10x fewer intrinsic carriers and far weaker band-to-band tunneling.
why: Junction generation current scales with n_i and GIDL is band-to-band tunneling at that edge; both collapse in a wide-gap pocket, targeting the 13 fA tail (fact 3) for 10-100x longer retention. Risk: antiphase domains and Ga/P cross-doping into the channel.

title: Crested tunnel barrier serves as two-terminal field-switched access
idea: Effect: field-sensitive tunneling through a crested (peaked) barrier. A Si3N4/AlN/Si3N4-type trilayer replaces the access channel; high bias pulls the central peak down (current rises ~10^12 over a 3x voltage change) so the node writes in ns at +/-3 V but leaks <1 aA at the +/-0.5 V hold and half-select bias.
why: 3D and leakage (facts 2, 3): two-terminal vertical stack layers into tiers without a lateral transistor; claims >=10 s retention. Risk: barrier wear and disturb.

title: Photoconductive switch from pulsed-power labs as an optically gated access device
idea: Pulsed-power and THz labs use photoconductive switches: wide-bandgap semiconductors that insulate in the dark and conduct when illuminated. Make the access element a GaN or ZnO photoconductive bridge under an on-chip SiN waveguide 'optical wordline'; dark off-current is set by a ~3.4 eV bandgap (sub-aA) and a ~1 ns light pulse opens it for read/write.
why: Removes the ~3 V wordline swing (fact 10) and the bandgap-limited leakage tail (fact 3); optical wordlines have no RC, allowing longer rows with fewer drivers (fact 7).

title: Atom-thin channel: 2D semiconductor access with no bulk to leak
idea: Inverts 'the access transistor is carved from bulk silicon': grow or transfer monolayer WSe2/MoS2 channels into a BEOL vertical gate-all-around access device; the 0.7 nm body has no junction volume, a 1.6-2 eV gap and full gate control, putting Ioff around 10^-19 A/um and allowing stacking above CMOS.
why: Retention 64 ms -> minutes (fact 3), near refresh-free, and stackable 3D tiers without a lateral silicon transistor (fact 2).

title: Vacuum-tube revival: nano vacuum-channel field-emission access switch
idea: Adapted from vacuum tubes and the thermos flask: replace the silicon access transistor with a gated nano vacuum channel (sharp Si or Mo emitter tip, 10-20 nm sealed vacuum gap, gate ring) that conducts by field emission only when the wordline raises the tip field. With the gate low, electrons must tunnel through the full vacuum barrier, so there is no junction, no GIDL and no subthreshold diffusion path.
why: Attacks the <=13 fA leakage tail (fact 3): off-current set by vacuum tunneling could be <1 aA, pushing retention from 64 ms toward minutes and cutting refresh energy >100x; risks are emitter wear, drive voltage and hermetic sealing at cell pitch.

title: Molybdenum buried wordlines exploit shorter electron mean free path
idea: Effect: electron mean-free-path size effect (Fuchs-Sondheimer/Mayadas-Shatzkes). Replace TiN/W buried wordlines with barrierless Mo or Ru (mean free path ~11 and ~7 nm vs ~19 nm for W), cutting 10 nm-line resistance ~30-40% and freeing the barrier's trench volume; faster wordline edges shorten each internal refresh burst. DDR/HBM pins, commands and timings stay unchanged.
why: Refresh time and resources (facts 3, resources): ~2x lower wordline RC, ~20-30% shorter refresh activity, and tungsten (China ~80%) removed from the array.

title: Chameleon's skin: electro-optic non-destructive readout of stored charge
idea: A chameleon displays its state as color. A thin barium titanate electro-optic layer beside each storage node lets the node voltage shift, via the Pockels effect, the resonance of a micro-ring on a row waveguide; reading a row means shining light through and detecting per-cell resonance shifts, with no bitline swing and no charge removed.
why: Non-destructive optical read removes bitline charging and restore, potentially >=10x lower read energy per bit and no read disturb; density of micro-rings is the major risk.

title: DirectFlash for DRAM: hyperscalers buy raw, retention-unscreened dies
idea: Some all-flash array vendors buy raw NAND and manage it themselves. Hyperscalers likewise buy DRAM dies that skip hot retention test, laser repair and retention binning, at a discount, and run them behind their own LDPC/CXL controller sized for 1% cell BER.
why: Cost and supply: retention test and burn-in tie up costly testers and scrap marginal dies; moving that job into the buyer's code adds several % usable supply and cuts test cost per bit.

title: Age-tracking sense reference counterweights expected charge decay
idea: TRIZ #8 Anti-weight: oppose the 'weight' of leakage with a counter-force. Because retention failures are overwhelmingly charged-to-discharged, the sense-amplifier reference (reference-cell charge or bitline precharge offset) is stepped down according to the known age of each row since its last restore (derived from the refresh counter), following the measured decay curve, so a partly drained '1' still reads and restores correctly.
why: Extends the usable refresh interval 2-4x (Fact 3) by spending the unused margin on the '0' side; costs a small reference DAC per sense-amp group.

title: Buy the rejects: harvest downbinned DRAM with remap firmware
idea: 10-person constraint: we cannot make bits, so we rescue them. Buy retention-failing or downbinned DRAM dies, plus decommissioned hyperscaler DIMMs that fail the 64 ms/85 C screen, at scrap prices. Re-grade them on an FPGA tester and sell them on CXL cards whose controller combines weak-row remap, extra refresh for only the weak rows, and spare capacity.
why: Scarce-resource and cost axes: a few percent of global output that is now scrapped or downbinned becomes usable supply at under 30% of contract price, with no fab.

title: Farm-equipment right-to-repair: open retention and repair command standard
idea: Adapted from the right-to-repair rules won for farm equipment: a JEDEC requirement backed by federal procurement rules that vendors publish the commands to read retention maps, trigger post-package repair and set refresh multipliers, so independent shops can repair and re-grade modules.
why: Third parties cannot repair retention-degraded modules today, so they are scrapped; open repair interfaces expand usable supply and seed U.S. refurbishment work without new fabs (fact 3, U.S. manufacturability).

title: ReLU-sparsity polarity mapping: zeros stored in the non-leaking state
idea: AI activation tensors are 50-90% zeros after ReLU. Map the dominant value to the cell state that cannot leak (discharged node, using true/complement bitline placement plus a per-row invert bit) and keep a per-row all-discharged flag so the controller skips refresh for rows holding no charged cells.
why: Fact 3: only charged cells need refresh, so for sparse AI data refresh energy drops by roughly the sparsity fraction (2-5x).

title: Second-life DDR4 behind CXL controllers with per-row refresh
idea: Hyperscalers retire millions of DDR4 RDIMMs that still work but whose retention tails have aged. Build a CXL Type-3 FPGA card that hosts eight retired DIMMs, profiles every row at intake, and runs per-row refresh plus strong ECC. Sell it as a far-memory tier; the prototype and pilot run fit within $1M and 24 months.
why: Adds usable capacity without new wafers (supply, capital and scarce-resource axes), with refresh tuned to measured retention rather than spec (fact 3).

title: Deuterium-hardened access stack starves variable-retention traps
idea: Scale jump down to the atomic nucleus: replace hydrogen with deuterium in the final forming-gas anneal and in SiN/SiO2 precursors around the access transistor and storage junction; the heavier Si-D bond resists breaking, so fewer interface and junction traps form over life and fewer metastable defects toggle, which is the source of variable retention time.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): VRT and trap-assisted GIDL dominate the <=13 fA tail; the isotope effect cuts hot-carrier trap generation 10-50x in logic, so a 2-4x tighter retention tail and longer refresh interval are plausible.

title: Magnify the log, minify the NV tier: per-store persistent journal
idea: Mirror every store into a 64 MB MRAM ring-buffer journal on the module (64 B appends via write combining) with periodic incremental snapshots to NAND; after power loss full DRAM state is rebuilt by snapshot plus journal replay.
why: Whole-DRAM persistence for ~0.5% added NV capacity with no change to the DRAM cell; the ring wear-levels itself.

title: Vertical charge-coupled memory: no switch per bit, just moving charge
idea: Inverts 'every bit needs its own access transistor': deposit a 200-layer gate/oxide stack (NAND-style, one hole etch), line each hole with a poly-Si or oxide channel, and clock the layer gates in 3 phases so charge packets march along the hole like a vertical CCD. Each hole holds ~60 bits and one sense/regeneration stage at the top restores packets as they circulate, so refresh is continuous and free.
why: No per-bit transistor, capacitor or litho: cost tracks 3D NAND (~$0.05-0.1/GB), ~100x below DRAM per GB; trade-off is serial access (~us to the far bit, high streaming bandwidth) and transfer-loss risk in poly channels.

title: Inverted HBM: logic die on top, DRAM tiers below
idea: Rearrange the stack order: put the hot base/logic die at the top of the stack, directly under the heatsink, and the DRAM tiers beneath it on the interposer, with logic power fed up through a dedicated power-via column in the DRAM dies. DRAM no longer sits in the heat path of the logic die.
why: Leakage roughly doubles every ~10 C; DRAM running 15-25 C cooler cuts refresh rate 2-4x and leaves the >85 C double-refresh range (facts 3, 6).

title: Bank-paired bitline charge recycling during refresh
idea: IFR: charge that falls in one bank is the charge that rises in another. Refresh banks in pairs offset by half a cycle, linking their bitline restore rails through a 2-4 step switched-capacitor ladder so bank A's discharge toward precharge directly supplies bank B's restore swing.
why: Fact 3: bitline swing is the biggest share of refresh energy; charge recycling recovers ~40-60% of it with no cell change.

title: Hermit-crab strategy: memory tiers built in idle display-TFT fabs
idea: Hermit crabs move into shells others built; repurpose idle Gen-6/8.5 oxide-TFT display lines (all <=400 C, already depreciated) to make low-leakage 1T1C oxide-TFT DRAM at ~0.8-1.5 um rules, diced into tiles for a CXL capacity tier, with conversion grants for US and allied display/solar fabs.
why: Oxide TFT retention of seconds makes refresh negligible; using no EUV and sunk capex gives a far-memory tier at roughly $5-30/GB, depending on design rule, that frees leading-edge DRAM for hot data and adds US-manufacturable supply.

title: Helium nanocavity gettering layer beneath DRAM arrays
idea: Box: standard cell x standard access x SA x array-wide buried layer x Si x MeV He implant + anneal forming nanocavities ~1 um below junctions. Cavity walls trap Fe, Cu and Ni that create mid-gap generation centers in storage junctions, the origin of many tail cells.
why: Shrinks the retention tail (fact 3) 2-5x; uses milligram-scale helium, negligible against the Qatar-constrained supply.

title: Atmospheric mist-CVD gallium oxide access transistors on sapphire panels
idea: TRIZ #29 Pneumatics and hydraulics: deposit corundum-phase alpha-Ga2O3 (Eg ~5.3 eV) channels from an ultrasonic aerosol of gallium acetylacetonate solution carried by gas at atmospheric pressure onto sapphire, with no vacuum tools, then pattern access transistors whose thermal generation leakage is effectively nil.
why: Ultra-wide gap gives retention far beyond 64 ms (Fact 3); atmospheric aerosol deposition slashes capital intensity (Fact 4). Gallium supply is China-concentrated, so a recycling loop is part of the plan.

title: Automotive LDMOS drift region at the storage-node junction
idea: Automotive power MOSFETs handle hundreds of volts by spreading the field over a lightly doped drift region. Give the access transistor's storage-node side a short graded drift extension with the buried-wordline edge acting as a field plate, so the peak field that drives GIDL and trap-assisted tunneling falls ~30-40%.
why: Fact 3: the <=13 fA tail comes from high-field trap-assisted tunneling, which depends exponentially on field, so tail-cell leakage could drop ~10x and the tail-set refresh interval stretches accordingly.

title: Two-threshold margin sensing during refresh learns each row's retention online
idea: TRIZ #20 Continuity of useful action: refresh is pure overhead, so make every refresh also a measurement. Sense amps perform a second, offset sensing pass during refresh; rows whose '1' signal has decayed past a warning threshold are promoted to a faster refresh bin and rows with large margin are demoted to slower bins, building a live per-row retention map that tracks VRT and aging.
why: Replaces worst-case 64 ms with learned bins (Fact 3): 4-8x fewer refreshes, robust to variable-retention cells that defeat one-time test profiling.

title: Airline departure board: compiler-published buffer lifetimes elide refresh entirely
idea: Airlines know every departure in advance and staff gates accordingly. AI accelerator compilers know statically when each activation or gradient buffer is next rewritten; they publish per-region lifetimes to the memory controller, which skips refresh for any row guaranteed to be rewritten or freed within tREFW.
why: Training activations live milliseconds, so 40-70% of HBM rows may never need refresh in such workloads, recovering much of the 10-20% bandwidth lost to refresh (fact 3).

title: Minify refresh to zero: tunnel-diode trickle latch per cell
idea: Stack a pair of nanoscale Esaki interband-tunnel diodes (Goto pair) on the capacitor top electrode; their N-shaped I-V creates two stable node voltages that continuously replace leaked charge with ~10 fA standby current, so the cell holds itself like SRAM at near-DRAM size.
why: Refresh eliminated; standby stays <2 mW for 16 Gb if diode valley currents are tuned to 10-100 fA.

title: Power-gate idle ranks once idle time beats the break-even
idea: Compute the break-even from first principles. A 64 GB DDR5 RDIMM in self-refresh burns ~0.5 W, while spilling and restoring 64 GB to NVMe costs ~2 nJ/B each way (~250 J), so any idle stretch beyond ~8 minutes is cheaper with the rank powered off. Add a hypervisor policy that compacts cold pages, spills them to NVMe or compresses them into active ranks, and cuts the rank's rails through the DIMM PMIC. Software and firmware, <$500k.
why: This removes retention energy entirely for idle capacity (overnight and diurnal troughs), attacking refresh's 16-33% share of idle power across the data center (fact 3).

title: Dynamic-mode 3D NAND: hold charge in the channel, not the trap
idea: Inverts 'NAND lines can only make nonvolatile flash': operate existing 300-layer 3D NAND strings as capacitorless floating-body cells, injecting holes by GIDL into the poly channel under a selected wordline (neighbors biased as barriers), sensing the Vt shift through the string and refreshing every ~1-10 ms; the trap layer is never programmed, so endurance is unlimited.
why: Taps existing, depreciated NAND fab capacity and flow, ~50-150x cheaper per GB than DRAM; trade-off is ~1-5 us latency, page-granular access and heavy refresh.

title: Swap electrostatic gating for piezoelectronic pressure-driven insulator-metal switch
idea: Substitute the gate field with mechanical pressure: a thin AlScN piezo actuator squeezes a pressure-sensitive insulator-metal transition layer (SmSe-type) between storage node and bitline. Under GPa-scale stress its resistance drops ~1e4-1e6; relaxed, it is a bandgap insulator.
why: Steep ~0.3 V switching breaks the wordline voltage floor, and the off state is a true insulator rather than a weakly-off transistor: ~10x wordline energy and long retention claimed.

title: Vertical NPN gain cell with storage on the floating base
idea: A BiCMOS cell puts the storage node on the floating base of a vertical bipolar transistor under the MOS access gate. A read pulses the emitter so collector current amplifies the stored charge by beta, roughly non-destructively.
why: A gain of 50-100 lets sub-fF residual charge be sensed, tolerating ~10x more decay before refresh, and it removes most restore energy.

title: Retention passport fused into every die, read by hosts
idea: Random stimulus 'passport': a document that travels with you and gets stamped at each border. Propose a JEDEC field in which each die fuses its per-bank retention class and temperature slope at test; the host reads the passport at boot and sets per-bank refresh, instead of every part inheriting the worst-case 64/32 ms spec.
why: Industry-wide policy that turns test data DRAM makers already collect into 2-4x fewer refreshes system-wide (fact 3) with no new silicon.

title: Full-restore sweep banks maximum charge before long idle periods
idea: Retention is t = dQ/I, and timing-limited activations often leave cells ~5-10% short of full VDD. Before a rank enters relaxed refresh or self-refresh, the controller sweeps every row with 2-3x tRAS/tWR so each cell banks its full charge, and only then lengthens the interval. This is pure controller timing work, prototyped on an FPGA DRAM platform for <$200k.
why: Raising the restored level from ~0.9 to ~1.0 VDD adds ~30% margin above the sense threshold, buying 20-40% longer refresh intervals for one cheap sweep (facts 1, 3).

title: Let the workload refresh: skip REF when activations cover every row
idea: Reverse who refreshes: in LLM inference every weight row is activated each token (~10-50 ms), and every ACT/PRE already restores its row. The memory controller keeps a per-bank activation-coverage bitmap over the refresh window and withholds REF for banks that were fully covered, falling back to normal REF the moment coverage lapses, while still issuing row-hammer RFM commands; firmware only, on unmodified DDR5/HBM.
why: Removes most refresh energy and the 10-20% refresh bandwidth loss (fact 3) for weight-streaming AI memory; no fab, firmware on existing controllers.

title: Van der Waals resonant-tunneling latch keeps each storage node topped up
idea: Integrate a series pair of graphene/hBN/graphene resonant-tunneling diodes (a Goto pair) in the capacitor top-electrode stack. Each storage node then has two stable voltages, and the RTD peak current continuously replaces what leaks away. The budget from first principles: peak current must exceed the 13 fA tail, and valley current must stay below ~0.7 pA per cell, the average power refresh spends per bit (46 fJ / 64 ms). The target is a peak-to-valley ratio of ~20 at the ~1 pA scale.
why: Refresh disappears entirely (fact 3) if BEOL-compatible 2D stacks meet the peak-to-valley target. Bistability becomes a property of the cell, not of the controller.

title: Leak-safe polarity coding; rows with no charged cells skip refresh
idea: TRIZ #13 The other way round: instead of fighting the direction leakage pushes, store data in the state leakage drives toward. A per-64-bit inversion flag chosen at write time minimises the number of charged cells; rows whose charged-cell count is zero (zeroed pages, sparse or quantised tensors) are flagged and never refreshed, and refresh priority follows charged-cell count.
why: Many rows are mostly zero (freed pages, sparse AI data): claim 30-60% fewer refreshes and lower exposure to the leakage tail (Fact 3).

title: Vertical CCD loops in channel holes with built-in refresh
idea: IFR: no cell needs a switch because the bit travels to the switch. 3D-NAND-style channel holes with 64-128 tier gates are clocked as a charge-coupled device; packets circulate around ~32-position loops and pass one regeneration/sense amplifier at the top every lap, so refresh is inherent and there is one transistor per loop.
why: Constraint: each bit is one gate crossing in a deposited stack, giving >10x density at 3D NAND cost per wafer; ~32 ns per lap keeps latency DRAM-class if loops stay short.

title: Volatile flash: a 2 nm tunnel oxide that forgets in seconds
idea: Inverts 'a charge-trap cell that loses data in seconds is a failed flash cell': on standard 3D NAND tools, thin the tunnel oxide to ~1.5-2 nm so programming uses low-field direct tunneling (~3-4 V, ~100 ns) that barely damages the oxide, accept seconds-scale retention, and refresh in large background bursts.
why: Direct tunneling targets 10^12+ endurance for a capacitor-free, transistor-free 3D cell at NAND-like cost (~100x cheaper per GB); trade-off: ~100 ns writes, us page reads, ~1 s refresh.

title: Coaxial nested capacitor shells: four cells in one hole
idea: IFR: one hole holds many cells. Conformally deposit four concentric storage electrodes separated by high-k and plate shells in one deep hole, each ending at a different height so a ring-shaped oxide-TFT access device wraps each shell's exposed top edge at its own level; one etch plus depositions makes four cells per hole.
why: Constraint: 4 cells per 4F^2 hex hole is ~6x versus 6F^2 planar, and a second hole tier reaches ~12x with mostly deposition steps; ultralow-leak ring TFTs offset the smaller per-shell capacitance.

title: Piano tuning: periodic field re-trim of sense-amplifier offsets
idea: Adapted from routine piano tuning: each sense amplifier has a small offset-trim capacitor bank whose setting is stored in non-volatile cells, and a maintenance routine re-measures offsets with known test levels every few months and re-tunes them as transistors drift.
why: Sense-amp offset consumes a large share of the retention signal margin; keeping it trimmed for life allows perhaps 30-50% more decay, so refresh intervals stay long as parts age (fact 3), and refurbishers re-tune instead of scrapping.

title: Deep-space LDPC pages: refresh at the 1% retention quantile
idea: CCSDS deep-space links decode reliably near 1e-2 raw BER. Store each 4 KB page as one LDPC codeword (~15% parity, decoder in the HBM base die or CXL controller) and set refresh where 1% of cells have decayed instead of where the last 1e-9 tail cell does; the median retention distribution is far longer than the tail, so the interval grows from 64 ms to ~1-2 s.
why: Fact 3: refresh energy and bandwidth loss fall ~15-30x and per-row profiling and VRT guardbands are no longer needed; costs ~15% parity and decode latency hidden behind page-granular access.

title: Shaker-channel ball-and-chain NEMS access gate
idea: Copying the K+ channel's N-type inactivation ball that plugs the pore, replace the access FET with a nanoelectromechanical gate: a conductive nanoball on a compliant SiN tether is pulled by the wordline field into a contact cavity bridging bitline and storage node, and the tether spring plus a self-timed 'inactivation' electrode retracts it, leaving a ~3 nm vacuum gap.
why: Off-state is vacuum tunneling (<1e-21 A vs the 13 fA tail), so retention goes from 64 ms to hours and the ~46 fJ/bit refresh and 10-20% bandwidth tax disappear; zero subthreshold slope also removes the need for a ~3 V wordline overdrive.

title: Eliminate refresh for ephemeral data: lifetime-tagged no-refresh DRAM regions
idea: Software tags allocations with a maximum lifetime (activations, gradients, KV-cache blocks consumed within milliseconds); the controller maps them to banks with refresh disabled, and a per-region epoch timer faults if data outlives the guaranteed retention bin. Data that dies before it decays is never refreshed.
why: AI activation traffic often lives <10-50 ms; removing refresh for 30-60% of HBM capacity eliminates the 16-33% idle-power refresh share and 10-20% bandwidth loss on those banks with no cell change.

title: Data that dies young: refresh-free banks for transient tensors
idea: Inverts 'every byte must be retained until overwritten': the compiler tags each AI tensor with its lifetime (activations and KV segments often live <10 ms), and the memory controller places them in banks whose refresh is masked off, guaranteeing reuse or overwrite within the profiled retention window; only weights and long-lived state sit in refreshed banks.
why: Removes refresh energy and bandwidth loss (fact 3) for most accelerator traffic (worth ~10-20% bandwidth and much of idle power) with only a per-bank refresh-mask command.

title: Sushi chef's freshness window: refresh-free ephemeral memory with expiry
idea: A sushi chef never stores fish past its window; it is served fresh. A new 'ephemeral' allocation class for activations, KV scratch and network buffers stamps each row with its write time; those rows are never refreshed, and the controller traps any read after the guaranteed retention window (e.g., 32 ms at the measured temperature) so software recomputes.
why: AI activations live microseconds to milliseconds; skipping refresh on them reclaims the 10-20% refresh bandwidth tax at high densities for the most bandwidth-hungry data.

title: Series dual-wordline vertical access with stack-effect leakage and AND addressing
idea: Po: every lock needs two keys. Put two independently driven gate rings in series on one vertical pillar channel, one on a row wordline and one on a column-group wordline; the cell opens only when both are high, so off leakage falls by the stack effect and half-selected cells see only one gate on.
why: Facts 3 and 9: stack effect cuts subthreshold leakage 10-30x and splits the drain field to curb GIDL; AND-addressing also blunts row hammer because an aggressor wordline only half-opens its neighbors.

title: Librarian fetches one book: row-and-column coincident access cell
idea: A librarian pulls one book, not the whole shelf. Each cell gets a second vertical access transistor in series, gated by a column-group select line, so a cell reaches its bitline only when both its row and its 64-bit group are selected; the other 127/128 of the row stay isolated, unread and unrestored.
why: Removes the 128x overfetch and the destructive restore of untouched cells (fact 8): activate energy per useful bit drops ~10-50x and row-hammer disturb shrinks; costs ~1.3-1.5x cell area unless the second device is stacked vertically.

title: Postal carrier rings one doorbell: BEOL TFT micro-wordline drivers
idea: A postal carrier rings one doorbell, not the whole building. Oxide-TFT micro-wordline drivers are stacked in the back end over the array, one per 16-cell wordline segment, AND-ing a global row line with a column-group line, so an access charges only 16 cells' gates and swings only 16 bitlines.
why: Wordline and bitline energy per access fall ~32-64x versus a 1k-cell segment, and the drivers take no silicon area (periphery is ~49% of die, fact 7).

title: Coulomb-blockade quantum-dot islands as the access switch
idea: Spin-qubit fabs already pattern ~5 nm silicon islands; put an array of ~100 parallel sub-3 nm Si dots in series with the storage node so the single-electron charging energy (>10 kT at room temperature at that size) blocks transport unless the wordline aligns the dot levels. Off-current then falls exponentially with charging energy instead of riding the thermionic subthreshold tail.
why: Fact 3: an off-state set by a Coulomb gap rather than Vt could cut the leakage tail >100x and remove most refresh; the parallel dot array is needed to reach ~0.5 uA on-current for 10 ns writes.

title: Bit-plane slicing puts NN weight LSBs in rarely refreshed rows
idea: Worse: protect every bit of a neural network equally. Flip: store weights transposed into bit planes; MSB planes go to normally refreshed rows and the low 4 bit planes to rows refreshed 16x slower, where rare flips cost under 0.1% accuracy.
why: Refresh energy for AI-resident memory (fact 3) down 40-60%.

title: Antiferroelectric gate with built-in bias trades retention for endurance
idea: Po: memory that forgets on purpose. Put a ZrO2-rich antiferroelectric layer in the gate stack of a single transistor with asymmetric work-function electrodes that shift its loop so one polarized state is metastable for ~1 s; the field-induced phase relaxes back on its own, giving a refreshed volatile 1T bit with much less fatigue than full ferroelectric switching.
why: Facts 1 and 3: capacitorless bit with refresh ~15x rarer than DRAM, aiming at 1e14+ endurance; goes beyond the prior nonvolatile HZO work.

title: Parametron-pumped refresh: global 2f pump restores charge without sensing
idea: Revive Goto's 1954 parametron, in which a pump at twice the signal frequency amplifies whichever phase is already present: give each cell a tiny MOS varactor coupled to its storage node and drive a global plate-line pump, so stored charge is parametrically amplified toward its own rail and bits are restored in place without row activation or sense amps.
why: Refresh costs ~46 fJ/bit and 10-20% of bandwidth (fact 3); in-place parametric restoration would make refresh bandwidth-free and cut its energy several-fold, because no bitlines swing.

title: Negative-capacitance HZO layer inside the buried-wordline gate stack
idea: Put a thin ferroelectric HZO film in series with the high-k gate dielectric of the buried-channel access transistor. Its negative capacitance amplifies gate-to-channel coupling and gives a sub-60 mV/dec subthreshold slope.
why: Allows Vt to rise ~200 mV at the same on-current, for 50-100x lower subthreshold leakage. Alternatively it lets the 3 V wordline boost drop (fact 10).

title: Token-cadence weight reads replace auto-refresh
idea: In LLM decode every weight row is activated each token (20-50 ms). A 180 nm controller or FPGA marks weight banks as refreshed by access, suppresses auto-refresh while cadence stays inside the retention window, and falls back to auto-refresh when traffic stalls.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth for the weight region drop to zero, recovering the 10-20% bandwidth tax at 32-64 Gb with no new silicon.

title: Substitute litho-defined pillars with self-ordered anodic alumina templates
idea: Substitute lithography for the vertical-channel array with anodized aluminum: self-ordered hexagonal pores ~15-25 nm wide, guided by a shallow imprinted pre-pattern. Vertical channels are grown inside the pores by selective H2-carrier epitaxy or ALD, and the alumina stays as the host for the gate dielectric.
why: The wet electrochemistry needs no rare gas and no EUV/DUV, and pore diameter is fixed by anodization voltage, tightening channel width and leakage spread while slashing capex.

title: EEPROM high-voltage module builds a thick-oxide, high-Vt access transistor
idea: Use the 1990s EEPROM HV process: 12-15 nm gate oxide, Vt ~1.3 V and channels of 0.5 um or more. EEPROM charge pumps boost the wordline to 5-6 V.
why: Off-leakage of ~1e-18 A gives minute-scale retention, so refresh is negligible. It trades density for a refresh-free tier made in any legacy fab.

title: Bank-to-bank bitline charge recycling during refresh bursts
idea: Box: standard cell x standard access x SA x charge-transfer switches linking bitlines of two banks refreshed in antiphase x in-array design x Si x zero masks. When bank A finishes restore, its high-side bitline charge is shared into bank B's bitlines before discharge, reusing up to half the swing charge.
why: Refresh energy (~46 fJ/bit, fact 3) and VARY supply current cut ~30-40% with only switches and timing.

title: Minify one-size refresh: JEDEC per-module retention negotiation field
idea: Push a JEDEC addition where each module publishes a measured, temperature-indexed retention table in SPD, re-measured by in-field self-test, and the controller negotiates tREFI from it instead of the fixed 64/32 ms rule.
why: Industry-wide 2-8x refresh reduction on most parts at zero silicon cost.

title: Konarka's moisture death avoided via roll-to-roll spatial-ALD ultrabarrier
idea: Konarka's roll-to-roll organic PV died largely from water and oxygen leaking through weak barriers. Deposit a 20 nm Al2O3/ZrO2 nanolaminate by R2R spatial ALD (WVTR <1e-6 g/m2/day) directly over the oxide access TFTs. It also blocks in-diffusing hydrogen, which acts as a donor and raises off-current.
why: Stops the leakage tail from drifting in the field, the main reliability risk of printed oxide memory, so a long refresh interval set at test stays valid for years.

title: Biased deep carrier-sink layer shields arrays from substrate leakage
idea: Scale shift of the analog guard ring (100 um) to every array mat: implant a deep, positively biased phosphorus collector layer under each mat inside a boron array well so thermally generated substrate electrons are collected before they diffuse into storage nodes.
why: Diffusion component of junction leakage (fact 3), dominant at 85 C: ~2-5x retention at high temperature using only B and P implants.

title: Substitute sputtered TiN/W wordline with ALD molybdenum nitride gradient
idea: Substitute the argon-sputtered TiN liner and CVD tungsten fill with thermal ALD Mo (MoO2Cl2 + H2, N2 purge). NH3 pulses near the trench top make the MoNx there lower in work function than the deep channel region, keeping Vt high while lowering the gate-drain field at the storage overlap.
why: The graded work function cuts GIDL ~5-10x without losing off-state Vt, and removes the tungsten (China ~80%) and argon-sputter dependence.

title: Idle rows nap in a charge-trap shadow inside the access gate
idea: Two timescales in one cell: the access transistor gate stack gets a thin SiN charge-trap layer; when a row has idled >1 s the controller applies one program pulse that copies each bit (via the storage-node-dependent channel potential) into trapped charge and stops refreshing the row; on the next access a Vt-shift sense restores the DRAM charge, so trap endurance is spent only on idle transitions (~1e6 over life).
why: Idle refresh power (16-33% of idle, fact 3) goes to ~0 for cold data, the majority of server capacity, while hot rows keep ns DRAM access.

title: Mg2Si thermoelectric film under the array cools only retention-critical mats
idea: Mg: deposit thin-film Mg2Si/Mg2Sn thermoelectric couples (abundant, non-toxic, no tellurium) in the backside BEOL with i-line patterning and drive them only under mats holding data in long-refresh mode, keeping those mats ~15-20 C below die temperature.
why: Leakage roughly halves per ~10 C, so 20 C of spot cooling allows ~4x longer refresh (fact 3); it pays only where Peltier power is below the refresh power saved, such as HBM above hot logic.

title: Substitute oxygen-precipitate gettering with implanted nanocavity gettering layer
idea: Substitute intrinsic oxygen-precipitate gettering with a buried band of nanocavities 1-2 um under the cell array, made by light-ion implant and anneal. Cavity walls bind Fe, Cu and Ni far more strongly than precipitates do, pulling the deep-level metal centers that create tail cells away from the storage junctions.
why: A few defect-bearing junctions dominate the retention tail; cleaning them pulls it toward the main distribution (2-4x tREF) and relaxes wafer-quality needs, so less depends on Cz quartz crucibles.
